messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 25-year-old journalist who had been proud of the parts of himself that made the work possible: his quickness, his curiosity, his willingness to walk into tense situations and come back with a clear account. That confidence fractured during an assignment covering a protest where police moved in aggressively after dark. He remembers the sound first as much as the images—the heavy rhythm of boots striking pavement behind him, officers shouting, the crackle of radios, a song from a nearby car still playing absurdly through the chaos. He was forced to the ground, pinned there, and for stretches of it he cannot give a coherent sequence; when he tries to tell it in session, he starts firmly and then loses the thread, falters, and stops. What remains with him comes in sharp pieces that feel more real than ordinary memory, and in those moments he hears the footsteps and shouted commands again as if they are happening now.

In the weeks afterward, seemingly ordinary moments began to hook directly into that night. If someone was walking behind him on the sidewalk, especially in the evening, his whole body tightened before he had fully registered why. Certain songs could do the same, especially if they were playing from a passing car or a store speaker, because they pulled up the sensory closeness of the arrest with a force he found hard to resist. Once those cues hit, the memory arrived vividly and with sound, and he was left scanning around him, looking over his shoulder again and again, trying to work out who was nearby and whether he could get away. He became especially wary in unfamiliar places, where he felt he could not judge exits or danger. Each time footsteps or a song set him off like this, the same thought landed with renewed force: this was what his life had become, a man who could be thrown back there by ordinary city sounds, and that seemed to him proof that he was no longer the steady reporter he had been. Living with that level of alarm gradually persuaded him that his fear was telling the truth about him: that something fundamental had been broken, and that he might never again be the steady, capable reporter he had been before. The danger he felt everywhere started to seem like proof that his life had been permanently narrowed. Even at work, where being in the field had once felt natural, entering a new neighborhood for an interview now meant checking behind him repeatedly and losing his concentration on the assignment itself.

As these reactions continued, Kwame began to make sense of them in increasingly bleak terms. He had come to believe that the trauma had destroyed his life, that the version of himself who could report clearly, move confidently, and stay open to the world was gone. Having decided that something fundamental in him had been broken, he entered streets, interviews, and even routine assignments already braced, as if his own damaged state meant danger was closer and harder to manage wherever he went. Once he was caught in that conviction, the memory seemed to come toward him more readily and with more force, as if his mind kept returning to the arrest to confirm the exact moment he had become this damaged person. The belief did not just follow the memory; it pulled him back into it, making the sounds and fragments feel even more immediate. After those fragments surged up, he began noticing echoes of them everywhere—the rhythm of someone approaching from behind, music drifting out of a car, the feel of evening on an unfamiliar block—so that more and more of the city took on the quality of a warning. Each time a pair of footsteps behind him sent him into alarm, or a song brought the scene back in a way that felt more real than the present, it seemed to prove to him that he was no longer capable of doing what had defined him. The memories did not feel like recollections he could place in the past; they felt like evidence that he had been permanently altered. He spoke about having once been a happy person and now feeling miserable as if that shift were complete and final.

Those beliefs changed how he lived. He started wearing concealing clothing—looser layers, hats, anything he thought might help him pass unnoticed on the street or while covering a story. He pulled away not only from reminders of people he had lost, but from anything that might stir feeling at all, good or bad, because emotion itself had begun to feel dangerous and unmanageable. He told himself this was practical: if he stayed flat, covered, and hard to read, maybe he could get through the day without being thrown back into the night of the assault. When his sense of danger rose, these habits intensified. On days when he was especially preoccupied with who might be behind him, he restricted his routes, avoided new locations whenever he could, and narrowed his life further. On those same days, the alertness itself seemed to pull the arrest closer; walking around keyed up and watchful, he would suddenly hear the officers' shouted commands again in his mind, vivid and immediate.

Over time, those strategies made his world smaller and his conclusions harsher. Avoiding songs, avoiding grief reminders, avoiding strong feeling, dressing to disappear—none of it restored his confidence. Instead, the constriction itself became another source of pain. He noticed he was taking fewer assignments that required initiative, hesitating with editors, and feeling ashamed that routine reporting now overwhelmed him. The more he lived as though he needed to hide, the more convincing it felt that his life had indeed been ruined and that he had lost the abilities that once mattered most to him. Because he was so busy managing exposure, his attention remained tuned to possible cues: footsteps in a hallway, music leaking from a car window, the atmosphere of a street he did not know. That constant vigilance made those triggers easier to detect, and once detected they summoned the same vivid, auditory memory again. Living with that level of threat day after day became its own kind of evidence to him that the damage was permanent; if he had to move through the world this braced, he thought, then maybe he truly was no longer someone who got to feel safe or capable.

His relationship has also tightened around these patterns. His partner has watched him go quiet when music comes on unexpectedly, watched him change routes or refuse unfamiliar places without explanation. Kwame finds it hard to explain because the memory fragments when he tries, and that failure leaves him feeling even more broken. Lately he has been struggling to complete field interviews because he cannot concentrate once he starts monitoring the environment, and he fears he is close to losing the career that anchored his identity. He is seeking help now because he can feel himself disappearing into a life organized around not being seen, not feeling, and not being caught off guard. What frightens him most is that this is permanent; what he hopes, cautiously, is that the night with the police will stop overrunning the present so he can work, love, and move through the city without bracing for it at every step.
